title: Quick check: Accessibility Testing

questions.prompt: In the context of “Accessibility Testing” and “Keyboard-only checks”, What makes a form control accessible to a screen reader and other users?
options: Semantic markup and a programmatically associated accessible name, such as a label linked to the input.
A placeholder alone for every required field.
A color difference with no other signal.
A clickable `div` with no keyboard interaction.
questions.answer_key: Semantic markup and a programmatically associated accessible name, such as a label linked to the input.
questions.explanation: Labels, semantics, focus visibility, keyboard behavior, and understandable errors are important parts of accessible UI.

questions.prompt: While implementing “Accessibility Testing”, How should language and text direction be represented?
options: Infer language only from a flag icon.
Force left-to-right direction for every locale.
Use the correct language metadata and direction for the localized content, and verify the whole layout.
Translate the page title but leave the content direction wrong.
questions.answer_key: Use the correct language metadata and direction for the localized content, and verify the whole layout.
questions.explanation: Localization includes language, routing, metadata, and possible right-to-left layout—not just translating a label.

questions.prompt: When reviewing “Accessibility Testing”, What is a robust way to test an interactive component?
options: Test keyboard and pointer use, visible focus, understandable state changes, and reduced-motion preferences where relevant.
Use animation as the only way to communicate a status.
questions.answer_key: Test keyboard and pointer use, visible focus, understandable state changes, and reduced-motion preferences where relevant.
questions.explanation: Accessibility checks should cover real interaction paths and should not rely only on visual color or motion.
